20 — Decision Traps

Status Quo Bias#

Heuristic
◆ The PatternPreference for the current state.

// Preference for the current state.

Status quo bias — preference for the current state of affairs; any change is perceived as a loss.

In investing:
• Never rebalancing a portfolio → allocation drifts far from target
• Sticking with an underperforming fund because switching feels risky
• Default 401(k) allocation → most employees never change it
• Holding inherited stocks forever regardless of fundamentals

Related to loss aversion: changing feels like a potential loss (of the current state), while the current state feels "free." It isn't.

Worked example

A 60/40 portfolio left alone through five good years for stocks ends at 75% stocks, 25% bonds. Nobody chose 75/25; it is what doing nothing produced. In retirement plans the effect is large: when Madrian & Shea (2001) studied a firm that switched to automatic enrolment, participation among new hires went from 37% to 86%, and most kept the default contribution.

Where it misleads
  • Inaction is sometimes optimal: trading costs and taxes make small adjustments not worth it (see Rebalancing in Risk & Portfolio).
  • A default can be a quiet recommendation; following it is not always bias.
  • The same force can be used for good — automatic escalation of savings works because people stay put (Thaler & Benartzi 2004).
In code
w0 = np.array([0.60, 0.40])                       # target: 60% stocks, 40% bonds
r = np.array([[0.20, 0.02], [0.15, 0.03], [0.25, -0.01], [0.10, 0.04], [0.18, 0.02]])   # five years, made up
grown = w0 * np.prod(1 + r, axis=0)
w_now = grown / grown.sum()                      # what you hold after five years of doing nothing

Sources
  • W. Samuelson & R. Zeckhauser, “Status Quo Bias in Decision Making”, Journal of Risk and Uncertainty 1(1), 1988
  • B. C. Madrian & D. F. Shea, “The Power of Suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) Participation and Savings Behavior”, Quarterly Journal of Economics 116(4), 2001
  • R. H. Thaler & S. Benartzi, “Save More Tomorrow: Using Behavioral Economics to Increase Employee Saving”, Journal of Political Economy 112(S1), 2004
